subject: english-language
title: Openings, Closings and Repair
welcome_lead: Conversation has architecture — entrances, exits and emergency exits. Step into Conversation Analysis.
meta_desc: Conversation Analysis openings, closings, repair sequences and discourse markers at A-Level.
final_note: You have surveyed the architecture of talk — and seen that even 'um' is doing precise work.

concepts.def: Conventional opening to talk: greeting + identification, especially in telephone calls (Schegloff).
Pre-closing tokens (well, anyway, okay) lead to terminal exchange (bye bye); closings are jointly negotiated.
Mechanisms for fixing trouble in talk — self-repair (I mean.), other-repair (Did you say Tuesday?).
Items like well, so, you know, right that organise discourse rather than carrying propositional content (Schiffrin 1987).
Listener feedback (mm, yeah, right) that signals attention without claiming the floor.
A linguistic device (sort of, kind of, maybe) that softens commitment to a proposition.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Schegloff (1968) studied telephone openings and showed how callers and answerers negotiate identification and recognition in highly conventional sequences.

A summons (ringing) calls for an answer, then both parties handle who-knows-whom — efficient micro-rituals.

Sacks and Schegloff showed that closing a conversation requires collaborative work: pre-closing tokens, arrangements (see you Friday) and finally terminal exchanges.

Cutting off without these sequences is socially marked — abrupt, even rude.

When something in talk is unclear, speakers initiate repair. Self-initiated self-repair (I mean Tuesday, not Monday) is preferred over other-initiated other-repair.

The system protects face while preserving mutual understanding.

mcqs.q: What is an adjacency pair in conversation analysis?
options: Adjacency pairs are two people who sit next to each other while talking.
A two-part sequence where the first part conditions the second — question/answer, greeting/greeting, request/acceptance-or-refusal. The second part is 'conditionally relevant' on the first.
Both terms mean the same — analysing language scientifically.
Adjacency pairs are pairs of synonyms in vocabulary lists.

mcqs.q: Are features of spoken language like 'um' and 'you know' signs of poor speech?
options: No — they are functional discourse markers and planning devices that help interaction flow, manage turn-taking and signal speaker meaning.
Adjacency pairs are pairs of synonyms in vocabulary lists.
Spoken language has no rules unlike written language.
Fillers and false starts show the speaker is uneducated.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between descriptive and prescriptive approaches to language?
options: Descriptivists describe written language and prescriptivists describe spoken language.
Both terms mean the same — analysing language scientifically.
Spoken language has no rules unlike written language.
Descriptivists describe how language is actually used; prescriptivists rule on how language ought to be used — modern linguistics is descriptivist.
